knowledge_point.title: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given Some Information About Another Point

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(\sqrt{338},\theta )$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(104,\theta +\pi ).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-13,-13).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-13}{-13}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $A$ lies in the third quadrant, we have $\theta =\pi +{\theta }_{R}=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$ Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(104,\frac{5\pi }{4}+\pi )=(104,\frac{9\pi }{4})=(104,\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =104\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =104\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =52\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =104\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =104\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =52\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(52\sqrt{2},52\sqrt{2}).$
